body_ar:
الحمد لله رب العالمين وصلى الله وسلم على نبينا محمد وعلى آله وأصحابه ومن اهتدى بهديه واستن بسنته إلى يوم الدين، السلام عليكم ورحمة الله وبركاته.

أما بعد فإن من الحروف ما هو مختص ببعض الأحكام، فلا بد من العناية به للعناية بتلك الأحكام التي تختص به، وهذه الحروف هي الميم والنون واللام فهذه الحروف الثلاثة تخرج عن قواعد الحروف لبعض الاختصاصات التي تختص بها، فاحتيج لبيان أحكام تختص بها، وقد عقد المؤلف رحمه الله تعالى هذا الباب لبيان أحكام الميم ولبيان حكم النون المشددة فقال:
body_en:
Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, and may God bless our Prophet Muhammad and grant him peace, and his family and his Companions and whoever has taken his guidance for guidance and his sunnah for a way, until the Day of Judgement. Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God and His blessings.

To proceed: among the letters there are some that have rulings peculiar to them, so they must be attended to in order that those rulings peculiar to them may be attended to. These letters are the mīm, the nūn and the lām: these three letters depart from the general rules of the letters on account of certain properties peculiar to them, and so there was a need to set out rulings peculiar to them. The author (may God, be He exalted, have mercy on him) set up this chapter to set out the rulings of the mīm and to set out the ruling of the doubled nūn. He said:

The published page carries only the opening excerpt of this tape; the Arabic breaks off and the full text is offered on the site as a downloadable Word document. The English ends exactly where the Arabic ends. Nothing has been supplied to complete it.
The Arabic stops at 'He said:', immediately before the lines of verse that were to be quoted. The verse is not in the source and nothing has been supplied for it; the English ends at the same point.

The word rendered 'rulings' here (aḥkām) is used in its recitational sense — the prescribed treatment of a letter in recitation, such as assimilation or nasalisation — not in the sense of the five legal rulings. Nothing in this excerpt attaches an obligation or a prohibition to an act.

al-Jazariyyah is the versified primer on Qur'anic recitation by Ibn al-Jazari, and 'the author' throughout this series is Ibn al-Jazari. The series title is left transliterated and untranslated. Articles 436-446 are tapes of this one series; their tape numbering in the titles does not run in the same order as the article IDs.
